capability.h1: How much useful work can AI complete reliably?
capability.summary: In benchmark tests, newer AI models complete longer technical tasks. It remains unclear how reliably they can handle all the tasks a job involves.
capability.selection: Use METR's tests to track progress on technical tasks at a specified success rate, with published estimates of uncertainty. The Remote Labor Index (RLI) adds evidence on completed projects beyond software.
capability.gap: Independent teams need to repeat tests of how reliably AI completes work from start to finish, including work beyond software.

sources.title: Remote Labor Index: projects meeting the reference standard
sources.locate: Performance Comparison, first row and legend; Core Metrics; original paper sections 3.2-3.4.
sources.label: Professional project completion
sources.date: Leaderboard read 13 October 2026; row evaluation date unclear
sources.finding: The leading listed agent scores 21.25% on the Remote Labor Index, which compares work produced by AI with reference examples from freelance projects.
sources.why: Compares completed professional work against a reference standard and provides project examples that readers can inspect.
sources.limit: These are selected test projects. The results do not show performance in actual jobs or whether clients would accept the work. Scale AI is a commercial research partner. Model release dates cannot establish when performance was measured or how it changed over time.
metrics: Not a share of jobs replaced
checks: Confirm 21.25% is the automation score, not Elo, and record the retrieval date.
Check grading, project denominator and evaluation setup before approving a historical curve.

sources.title: METR task-completion horizons at 80% success
sources.locate: Definition, Methodological Details and Updates; linked TH1.1 YAML, all records released from 2023 onward, metrics.p80_horizon_length and release_date.
sources.label: Reliability on longer tasks
sources.finding: At 80% success, the estimated task horizon rises from under one minute for GPT-4 (March 2023) to about three hours for Claude Mythos Preview (early, April 2026). This measure describes task length by how long the work takes people. The chart includes all 23 tested models released from 2023 onward.
sources.why: Relates AI's success rate to task length, measured by the time people need for the work. Results and estimates of uncertainty are available to download.
sources.limit: The tests cover technical tasks. They do not measure performance across whole jobs or how long an AI agent runs. The latest point has a wide 95% interval of 1.6-6.6 hours, showing substantial uncertainty in the estimate. The dates shown record model releases; they do not give the dates of evaluation. The tracker is no longer actively updated.
checks: Check the definition and stopped-update notice: task difficulty is not unattended runtime.
In the linked YAML, check all release dates, p80_horizon_length estimates and 95% intervals against the downloadable chart data.

adoption.h1: How common is regular AI use at work?
adoption.summary: The share of US employees using AI regularly rose from 11% in May 2023 to 32% in August 2026. How much work they hand over to AI remains unclear.
adoption.selection: Use Gallup's repeated surveys to track frequent AI use among US employees. Eurostat adds context on EU businesses. The measures cover different groups and use different definitions, so they must be interpreted separately.
adoption.gap: Track the share of work people hand over to AI, how they check its output, and whether they can still do the work without it.

sources.title: Gallup regular workplace AI use
sources.locate: Use of AI table, Frequent AI users column, eight rows from 5/1/23 to 8/1/26; Survey Methods above the table.
sources.label: Regular workplace AI use
sources.finding: The share of US employees using AI at work a few times a week or more rose from 11% in May 2023 to 32% in August 2026, a 21-percentage-point increase.
sources.why: Gallup repeats surveys of employees across occupations, using a sampling method in which each eligible employee has a known chance of selection. The frequent-use category distinguishes regular use from occasional experimentation.
sources.limit: The survey covers US employees aged 18+ working for organisations. Employees report their own AI use; the answers do not measure how much work is automated or how much people depend on AI. The table is newer than parts of the surrounding text and does not provide uncertainty intervals for each survey round.
metrics: A few times a week or more, May 2023
A few times a week or more, August 2026
checks: Check all eight Frequent AI users values and dates; daily users are included, not added separately.
Confirm US employee eligibility; do not call this a share of all adults, work hours or automated tasks.

sources.title: Eurostat enterprise AI use
sources.locate: Opening paragraph and Methodological notes in the dated news release; Data sources and Netherlands break note in Statistics Explained.
sources.label: AI use by EU businesses
sources.finding: 20.0% of covered EU enterprises used AI in 2025, up from 13.5% in 2024.
sources.why: Provides official, repeated measurements outside the US and clearly defines which businesses are included.
sources.limit: The survey covers businesses with 10 or more people in covered sectors, so the smallest firms are excluded. Its definition of AI extends beyond generative AI. A new AI category in 2025 and a break in the comparability of the Netherlands data complicate year-to-year comparisons.
checks: Verify both annual values and the 10-person cutoff in the release.
Check sectors, AI definition and the Netherlands break before interpreting the change.

handover.h1: How much work do people hand over to AI?
handover.summary: In May 2026, 48.6% of classified Claude chat and Cowork conversations were labelled automation, meaning AI was asked to complete a task. The data do not show whether people checked or used the output.
handover.selection: Use Anthropic's conversation data to distinguish asking AI to complete tasks from working with it. The UK regulator survey adds provisional evidence from financial services on how independently AI makes decisions.
handover.gap: Independent research across providers is needed to show which decisions AI makes, which people review, and which people can reverse.

sources.title: Anthropic Economic Index: automation and augmentation
sources.locate: June release CSV: May 2026, GLOBAL, overall, collaboration_bucket_automation_pct and collaboration_bucket_augmentation_pct. Data documentation defines metrics and platform coverage.
sources.label: Handing over tasks or working with AI
sources.date: Claude chat and Cowork, May 2026; June release
sources.finding: Among conversations assigned either mode, 48.62% were classified as automation, where AI is asked to complete a task, and 51.38% as augmentation, where people work with AI. The 2.61% labelled 'None' is excluded from the total used to calculate these shares, as verified by adding up the component categories.
sources.why: Conversation patterns provide evidence about how people hand over work that user counts alone cannot show. The underlying data are available to download.
sources.limit: The categories come from one provider's automated classification system. An automation label does not show whether AI acted independently or whether a person checked its work. May 2026 includes chat and Cowork; changes in how conversations were sampled prevent a simple comparison with older releases.
metrics: Automation among conversations assigned either mode
checks: Check the May GLOBAL overall CSV rows and normalized bucket denominator; unclassified conversations are excluded.
Review the provider classification and distinguish automation from decision autonomy or human review.

sources.locate: Section 1.2 Methodology; executive-summary Automated decision-making bullets; section 2.5 and Chart 7.
sources.label: AI decision-making in financial services
sources.finding: The survey distinguishes AI that automates part of a process from AI that acts fully independently. Before highlighting percentages, it is necessary to resolve whether they refer to firms or to individual uses of AI.
sources.why: A survey independent of AI providers examines how much of a process AI handles and how independently it acts.
sources.limit: Firms report on their own use in one sector. The survey does not count individual decisions. The chart subtitle and report text differ on whether percentages refer to firms or uses of AI; the result remains provisional until this is resolved.
checks: Read section 2.5 and methodology; confirm the 118 respondents and definitions.

work.h1: How is employment changing for younger workers?
work.summary: In the ADP payroll sample, employment among ages 22–25 fell 12.8% in the most AI-exposed occupations from November 2022 to August 2026. Employment in the least-exposed group rose 8.1%. AI exposure describes how closely job tasks match AI capabilities. These trends do not establish that AI caused the changes.
work.selection: Use Stanford/ADP's monthly payroll data to compare employment by age and AI exposure, showing all five exposure groups, called quintiles. The Danish study of workplaces encouraging chatbot use adds a different finding. Its population, outcome and period differ, so it needs separate interpretation.
work.gap: Link firms' AI adoption to hiring and training for junior workers, using comparisons that help distinguish AI's effects from other labour market changes.

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
sources.locate: Employment Index by Age Group and AI Exposure; September 2026 data package, Early Career 1 (22-25), all five quintiles, November 2022 = 100.
sources.label: Young workers in jobs exposed to AI
sources.date: September 2026 dashboard release; data through August 2026
sources.finding: From November 2022 to August 2026, the most-exposed quintile's employment index fell from 100 to 87.23; the least-exposed rose to 108.1, among ages 22-25 in the ADP sample. The index shows employment relative to its starting level. Quintiles group occupations by how closely their tasks match AI capabilities.
sources.why: Allows repeated comparisons of employment by age and AI exposure, with detailed discussion of other possible explanations for the changes.
sources.limit: The data describe employment trends without proving that AI caused job losses. Exposure measures the match between job tasks and AI capabilities; it does not establish actual AI use. Which workers enter the sample, their education and earlier employment trends all affect interpretation.
checks: Check the September package, ages 22-25, quintile definitions, baseline and all 60 monthly values.
Do not apply the earlier pooled 19% June shortfall to this chart's extreme-quintile August endpoints.

sources.label: Chatbot use and young workers in Denmark
sources.finding: Workplaces encouraging chatbot use showed no extra decline in their share of workers aged 22-25 through 2024.
sources.why: Links information about chatbot adoption to employment records, including whether workplaces encouraged chatbot use.
sources.limit: Workplaces were not randomly assigned to encourage chatbot use. The study covers a different country and period from the US study, and it cannot rule out later job losses.
metrics: Not a test of later US effects

Check the linked survey/register design; do not call encouragement randomized.

share.h1: How much economic output goes to workers?
share.summary: The ILO estimates that workers' income as a share of global economic output (GDP) fell from 53.0% in 2015 to 52.6% in 2025. The period begins before widespread generative AI use, and the comparison does not establish AI's effect.
share.selection: Use the ILO's global labour income share for international coverage, including income from self-employment. The BLS measure for the US nonfarm-business sector is updated more often. Its coverage differs, so it belongs in a separate comparison.
share.gap: Measure changes in workers' income alongside actual AI adoption within firms and sectors, using definitions that stay comparable over time.

sources.title: Labor share at its lowest level, 52.8 percent, in second quarter 2026
sources.locate: BLS Economics Daily, September 15, 2026: opening paragraph and Chart Data table; FRED PRS85006173 unit label.
sources.label: Workers' share of US nonfarm-business output
sources.finding: Labour compensation, which includes workers' pay and benefits, was 52.8% of US nonfarm-business output in Q2 2026, the lowest in this BLS series, which begins in 1947.
sources.why: Directly measures the share of output paid to workers, with an established record extending well before generative AI.
sources.limit: The measure covers one sector as a whole. It does not describe typical pay or identify AI's effect. The remaining output includes more than profit. FRED also publishes an index that tracks changes relative to a base period; that index cannot be read as a percentage share of output.
metrics: Nonfarm-business output paid as labour compensation
checks: Confirm the 52.8% level, quarter, sector and series start in BLS Chart Data.
Check numerator/denominator and distinguish percent of output from the FRED index.

sources.title: The world of work and the 2030 Agenda: a ten-year review
sources.locate: March 19, 2026 ILOSTAT review, Labour's share of the economy is shrinking. Both endpoints come from this release.
sources.label: Workers' share of global economic output
sources.finding: Global labour income share, the share of global economic output (GDP) going to workers, was 53.0% in 2015 and 52.6% in 2025: down 0.4 percentage points. The ILO describes partial recovery after a sharp decline in 2023.
sources.why: Extends coverage beyond the US and includes estimated income from the work of self-employed people.
sources.limit: These estimates rely on statistical models and may be revised. Two endpoints leave the annual path between them unknown. Figures from different report releases should not be joined into a trend, and this GDP-wide share cannot be compared directly with the BLS sector measure. The figures do not establish an effect of AI.
checks: Check both endpoints in the March 2026 release; do not substitute the older 2014-2024 vintage.
Confirm definition and modelled-estimate status; obtain annual data before replacing the two-endpoint chart with a line.

skills.h1: How well can people do the work without AI?
skills.summary: In one classroom trial, unrestricted GPT reduced later exam scores without AI by 5.4 points out of 100; a guided tutor showed no detectable difference. Evidence on how skills change over the long term remains limited.
skills.selection: A classroom trial tests what students learn when assessed without AI. A review combining results from many experiments examines when human judgement adds to AI performance. Neither measures long-term skill loss across society.
skills.gap: Follow the same people over time, testing what they can do both with and without AI.

sources.label: Learning without AI
sources.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
sources.finding: After the study's statistical adjustments, the difference in exam scores without AI was -5.4 points out of 100 for unrestricted GPT, about 17% relative to the average in the no-AI group. The guided tutor estimate was -0.4 points. That difference was not statistically significant, so the study did not detect a clear effect on exam scores for the tutor.
sources.why: The combination of random assignment and an exam taken without AI distinguishes help during practice from learning that lasts beyond the task.
sources.limit: The study covers one school setting with a short follow-up. It cannot establish permanent skill loss or effects across the wider population. The 17% compares the score difference with the no-AI group's average score; it is a relative change and must not be read as percentage points.
sources.locate: Table 1 column 2: coefficients -0.054/-0.004, SEs 0.022/0.013, control mean 0.321. Multiply by 100 for score points; chart intervals are calculated as estimate +/- 1.96 SE.
checks: Confirm the 17% relative difference and the no-AI comparison group.
Keep the tutor result and short follow-up alongside the harm finding.
metrics: Unaided exam score: unrestricted GPT vs no AI

sources.label: How people and AI perform together
sources.citation: Vaccaro, Almaatouq & Malone (2024), Nature Human Behaviour
sources.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.finding: On average, people working with AI performed better than people working alone. They performed worse than whichever did better on its own: people or AI. Results varied substantially by task.
sources.why: Combines evidence from many experiments and keeps two easily confused comparisons separate. Standardized effects put performance differences from different tasks on a common scale.
sources.limit: The experiments measure performance on tasks. They do not track how a person's skills change over time. Much of the evidence predates current generative AI.
checks: Confirm 106 experiments and the two different baselines.
Check that the page does not describe poorer teamwork as long-term deskilling.
metrics: Standardized effect vs the better of human or AI alone

culture.h1: How much attention goes to AI-made content?
culture.summary: Deezer reports that fully AI-generated music accounts for 1–3% of recorded streams and over 50% of uploads on peak days. Fraudulent streams and the platform's recommendation rules make it harder to tell how much attention people give this music.
culture.selection: Pair Deezer's repeated reports on uploads and listening with an independent experiment on how AI affects the variety of creative work. No single source covers culture as a whole.
culture.gap: Measure what people actually read, watch and hear, and whether human creators maintain their income and influence.

sources.label: AI music: uploads and listening
sources.title: Deezer will let you fully exclude AI-generated music from your streaming experience
sources.finding: Deezer reports fully AI-generated tracks exceed 50% of uploads on peak days, but account for 1-3% of streams.
sources.why: Uses repeated reports from the platform to distinguish the amount of AI music uploaded from the amount played.
sources.limit: The figures come from one platform using its own AI detector. Recorded streams may include fraudulent activity, and the report does not specify whether the figures were adjusted for it. Recommendation rules also affect listening. Uploads on peak days do not show the average across days.
sources.locate: Notes to editors; FAQ date note
checks: Keep 'on peak days', the August 2026 data date, and the 1-3% stream denominator.
Confirm the fraud and recommendation-policy caveats; do not generalize to all music.

sources.label: Creativity and variety in stories
sources.title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
sources.finding: AI-assisted stories received higher creativity ratings, but were more similar to one another than stories written without AI.
sources.why: An independent experiment tests how AI assistance affects creativity ratings and similarity between stories. The researchers registered their study plan in advance.
sources.limit: The experiment involved 293 writers producing short stories in one study. It does not establish declining diversity across culture or over time.
sources.locate: Results; Figures 2 and 4; Materials and Methods
checks: Confirm the 293 writers and distinction between reader ratings and text similarity.
Keep the creativity benefit as well as the reduced-diversity finding.

institutions.h1: Who makes the decisions when governments use AI?
institutions.summary: The US inventory records 3,611 reported uses of AI. It does not measure how many decisions AI makes or how much control people retain. Its CSV data file explicitly marks 1,480 as deployed or piloted; 338 have no development stage recorded.
institutions.selection: Pair the official inventory of reported AI uses with one example of a system in operation. Readers can inspect both sources, but neither independently audits all safeguards.
institutions.gap: For specific AI systems with major consequences for people, publish how many decisions they make, how often people review or override them, and what happens when people appeal.

sources.title: 2025 Federal Agency AI Use Case Inventory
sources.locate: 2025 inventory README, Summary and agency-table TOTALS; dictionary development_stage, is_high_impact and hi_appeal_process.
sources.label: US federal AI inventory
sources.citation: US Office of Management and Budget (2025 inventory)
sources.date: 2025 inventory; CSV pinned to 14 May 2026 commit
sources.finding: The CSV data file contains 3,611 rows: 1,040 deployed, 440 pilot, 1,479 pre-deployment, 314 retired and 338 with no development stage recorded. These stages distinguish systems in use, in trials, being prepared for use or taken out of use. The README's 1,818 deployed/piloted total includes cases with no stage recorded and cannot be reproduced using only explicit stage labels.
sources.why: Provides an official starting point that readers can reproduce, with public details about reported uses and definitions of development stages.
sources.limit: The inventory counts reported uses of AI. It does not count individual decisions or verify safeguards through an audit. Reporting rules change, and a missing answer does not necessarily mean a protection is absent.
metrics: Individual reported use cases, all stages
Explicitly deployed or in pilot; 338 stages missing
checks: Reconcile README's 1,818 with 1,480 explicit deployed/pilot CSV rows plus 338 blank stages; inspect data-sourcing notes.
Check stage and safeguard-field definitions; do not count blank fields as failed safeguards.

sources.title: Live Facial Recognition Annual Report September 2025
sources.locate: Annual Report September 2025: PDF page 5, Summary of Results; PDF pages 15-16, False alerts data.
sources.label: AI alerts and human action
sources.finding: London police reported 2,077 facial-recognition alerts, including 10 false alerts. Officers review alerts before deciding whether to approach someone.
sources.why: Shows reported results from a system in operation, including how officers check AI alerts before taking action.
sources.limit: The evidence comes from one police force reporting on its own system. It does not fully measure how often officers override alerts or how often the system misses a match, known as a false negative. It also provides no independent assessment of bias. An arrest does not establish that a person was convicted.
checks: Read PDF page 5 for the period and totals; keep alerts separate from arrests.
Read false-alert details on pages 15-16; do not infer a full override or false-negative rate.

influence.h1: How much say do people have in AI's role in their lives?
influence.summary: 57% of US adults reported little or no control over AI's use in their lives in June 2025. This measures how much control people feel they have. It has not been validated as a measure of their actual power to make decisions.
influence.selection: Use a representative public survey to describe people's sense of control and a clearly labelled exploratory study to examine behaviour in conversations. These offer indirect evidence about people's influence; they have not been validated as an overall measure.
influence.gap: Connect people's reported control to real choices: whether they can refuse AI use, appeal or reverse a decision, or act without AI.

sources.label: People's sense of control over AI
sources.title: AI in Americans' lives: Awareness, experiences and attitudes
sources.finding: 57% of US adults said they had little or no control over whether AI was used in their lives; 61% wanted more control.
sources.why: Uses a sampling method in which each eligible adult has a known chance of selection and publishes its questions and methods. The questions address people's sense of control over AI in their lives.
sources.limit: The survey measures how much control people feel they have. It does not observe their actual power to make decisions. It covers one country at a single point in time and cannot establish a decline caused by AI.
sources.locate: Section on control over AI; linked topline and methodology
checks: Match 57% and 61% to their separate questions and June 2025 fieldwork.
Keep 'felt control' distinct from actual power or proven harm.

sources.label: Potential loss of control in AI conversations
sources.title: Who's in Charge? Disempowerment Patterns in Real-World LLM Usage
sources.finding: Automated analysis flagged a small minority of conversations as having severe disempowerment potential: a risk that people lose control over their beliefs, values or actions.
sources.why: Defines conversation patterns that may indicate a loss of control over beliefs, values or actions. This gives researchers a way to study the potential risk.
sources.limit: The study uses the company's automated classification systems on one service. A flagged risk does not confirm harm or lasting loss of influence. Independent researchers need to repeat the study to test whether its findings hold.
sources.locate: Measuring disempowerment; Prevalence and patterns; paper methods
checks: Check the classifier validation and the distinction between potential and actual harm.
Confirm that conversation rates are not presented as rates of affected people.
